notes.4373: Line 4374: qui ains ains, literally 'who first, first', i.e. each rushing to be first.
notes.840: Line 843: Saint Richier is Saint Riquier. Line 854: as written, the emperor speaks to Naimes; a reply by Naimes interpreting the dream might be expected. Line 855: Montiblier not identified (the form recalls Montpellier).
notes.1444: Line 1447: maïsté, the divine Majesty, God enthroned.

nodes.text: “Barons,” said the emperor, “I am much troubled
that my legs and feet are all swollen.
Last night I dreamed a dream, I will not deny it to you:
it seemed to me, by the faith I owe Saint Riquier,
that we were in France, at Paris, in the orchard.
Such a fair people came out from there without delay,
as if they were angels, who must blaze with light.
All of them together were falling at my feet,
and you, with great love, raised them up;
and then I saw the cloud go back toward the sky.
After that I saw it rain and hail upon you,
and the white snow fall in great clumps;
there was more of it on you, I will not hide it from you,
and you gave a great share of it to the barons, the knights.”
“Naimes,” said the emperor, “if it please God, this will be good.”
After these words he looks at the plains of Montiblier;
he sees the young men coming, who were laden,
“Let us leave this old man, who has gone quite senile;
may his body be given over to a hundred thousand devils!”
Then here come Ganelon and his companion Hardré,
Thibaut and Alori, Malvaisin and Mauré.
May the Lord who suffered on the cross confound them!
that I may yet see Gui, the young knight,
and the help from France that I long for so much.”
Up toward the sky he began to look;
he saw the sky open as far as the Majesty,
and a most holy cross that gave out great brightness;
four winged angels hold it on every side.
The emperor was afraid, and bowed down low.
Saint Gabriel the angel came down to him;
he speaks into his ear, quietly, in secret:
“Emperor of France, listen to me:
have no fear, you are in safety,
for he who brought you here will lead you.”
The emperor hears him and takes heart again;
he bowed toward heaven, and at once turned away.
They all go out of the town without any delay,
and they do so at once, racing each other, with shouting.
And Charlemagne lay down on the grass in the meadow,
and has made a prayer, well made and well spoken,
that the town be brought to such a state
that it would never again be coveted by these men or by anyone else.
Then you would not have gone half a league
before the city has all sunk into the abyss,
and it is all brimming with water up over the walls,
and it is a good deal blacker than melted pitch,
and the walls are red as a pure rose;
those who go into that country see it still.
When the princes see this, it pleases them marvellously;
each has turned his face toward the East.
